Under GDPR, GDPR The relationship between GDPR and a Processor is characterized by specific obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities directly imposed upon the Processor by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). A processor is subject to the GDPR for any given processing operation, with its role and duties explicitly defined within the regulation. This subjection is set forth in Article 3 of the GDPR, which establishes its territorial scope and applicability, even extending to non-EEA processors when they are engaged by third-country companies. In such cases, these processors must also comply with Article 28 and Chapter V of the GDPR. The GDPR directly imposes various obligations on processors, detailing their responsibilities concerning personal data protection. Processors must ensure compliance with these requirements, particularly by adhering to the instructions provided by controllers. Key responsibilities include compliance with Article 30 (records of processing activities), Article 32 (security of processing), Article 35 (data protection impact assessment), and Article 36 (prior consultation with a supervisory authority) regarding risks. Processors are also subject to GDPR obligations relating to their liability for sub-processors, as outlined in Article 28(4). Furthermore, the GDPR requires processors to implement appropriate security measures and outlines their obligations regarding data breaches and notifications, including the requirement to notify any breach to their controller. Supervisory Authorities (SAs) have the power to take action against a processor for infringing GDPR provisions. The regulation categorizes various infringements that can lead to fines for processors. Certifications under the GDPR are also issued to data processors, further emphasizing their direct accountability and the regulatory oversight they are subject to. These collective requirements define the responsibility and liability of the processor under the GDPR.<SEP>The GDPR, specifically Article 60(10), imposes duties on the processor.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for ensuring data processing adheres to GDPR provisions.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for compliance with the GDPR and must be able to demonstrate it.<SEP>The processing by a processor is governed by a contract or legal act that ensures compliance with GDPR articles. Processor.

Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.
Under GDPR, GDPR Processing activities must comply with the GDPR. Processing.
Under GDPR, Employees' Personal Data Employees' personal data may be processed for the purpose of the termination of the employment relationship. Termination of the Employment Relationship.

Under GDPR, Personal Data The relation "(Personal Data, Processor)" defines the role and responsibilities of a Processor in handling Personal Data. A Processor is an entity that processes personal data strictly on behalf of and under the instructions of a Controller, operating as an agent in managing, extracting, handling, and transferring this data. Key duties include the implementation of robust security measures to protect the personal data entrusted to them. Processors are authorized to perform operations involving personal data, and individuals working under the direct authority of the Processor are also permitted to process such data. Upon the termination of processing activities, the Processor is generally obligated to either delete or return the personal data to the Controller, unless a legal requirement necessitates its storage. Furthermore, a Processor may transfer personal data, and within the context of the EU, they might even make personal data accessible to a third-country authority. Processor.

Under GDPR, Final Decision The final decision of the competent supervisory authority will be addressed to the processor.<SEP>The processor has duties to ensure processing activities comply with the final decision, as per Article 60(10) GDPR.<SEP>The Processor shall take necessary measures to ensure compliance with the Final Decision. [Source: EDPB_guidelines_202007_controllerprocessor_final_en] "Adopted - After public consultation 1 Guidelines 07/2020 on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR Version 2.1 Adopted on 07 July 2021 Adopted - After public consultation 2 Version history Version 2.1 20 September 2022 Minor corrections Version 2.0 7 July 2021 Adoption of the Guidelines after public consultation Version 1.0 2 September 2020 Adoption of the Guidelines for public consultation Adopted - After public consultation 3 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The concepts of controller, joint controller and processor play a crucial role in the application of the General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR), since they determine who shall be responsible for compliance with different data protection rules, and how data subjects can exercise their rights in practice. The precise meaning of these concepts and the criteria for their correct interpretation must be sufficiently clear and consistent throughout the European Economic Area (EEA). The concepts of controller, joint controller and processor are functional concepts in that they aim to allocate responsibilities according to the actual roles of the parties and autonomous concepts in the sense that they should be interpreted mainly according to EU data protection law. Controller In principle, there is no limitation as to the type of entity that may assume the role of a controller but in practice it is usually the organisation as such, and not an individual within the organisation (such as the CEO, an employee or a member of the board), that acts as a controller. A controller is a body that decides certain key elements of the processing. Controllership may be defined by law or may stem from an analysis of the factual elements or circumstances of the case. Certain processing activities can be seen as naturally attached to the role of an entity (an employer to employees, a publisher to subscribers or an association to its members). In many cases, the terms of a contract can help identify the controller, although they are not decisive in all circumstances. A controller determines the purposes and means of the processing, i.e. the why and how of the processing. The controller must decide on both purposes and means. However, some more practical aspects of implementation (“non-essential means”) can be left to the processor. It is not necessary that the controller actually has access to the data that is being processed to be qualified as a controller. Joint controllers The qualification as joint controllers may arise where more than one actor is involved in the processing. The GDPR introduces specific rules for joint controllers and sets a framework to govern their relationship. The overarching criterion for joint controllership to exist is the joint participation of two or more entities in the determination of the purposes and means of a processing operation. Joint participation can take the form of a common decision taken by two or more entities or result from converging decisions by two or more entities, where the decisions complement each other and are necessary for the processing to take place in such a manner that they have a tangible impact on the determination of the purposes and means of the processing. An important criterion is that the processing would not be possible without both parties’ participation in the sense that the processing by each party is inseparable, i.e. inextricably linked. The joint participation needs to include the determination of purposes on the one hand and the determination of means on the other hand. Processor A processor is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or another body, which processes personal data on behalf of the controller. Two basic conditions for qualifying as processor exist: that it is a separate entity in relation to the controller and that it processes personal data on the controller’s behalf. The processor must not process the data otherwise than according to the controller’s instructions. The controller’s instructions may still leave a certain degree of discretion about how to best serve the Adopted - After public consultation 4 controller’s interests, allowing the processor to choose the most suitable technical and organisational means. A processor infringes the GDPR, however, if it goes beyond the controller’s instructions and starts to determine its own purposes and means of the processing. The processor will then be considered a controller in respect of that processing and may be subject to sanctions for going beyond the controller’s instructions. Relationship between controller and processor A controller must only use processors providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures so that the processing meets the requirements of the GDPR. Elements to be taken into account could be the processor’s expert knowledge (e.g. technical expertise with regard to security measures and data breaches); the processor’s reliability; the processor’s resources and the processor’s adherence to an approved code of conduct or certification mechanism. Any processing of personal data by a processor must be governed by a contract or other legal act which shall be in writing, including in electronic form, and be binding. The controller and the processor may choose to negotiate their own contract including all the compulsory elements or to rely, in whole or in part, on standard contractual clauses. The GDPR lists the elements that have to be set out in the processing agreement. The processing agreement should not, however, merely restate the provisions of the GDPR; rather, it should include more specific, concrete information as to how the requirements will be met and which level of security is required for the personal data processing that is the object of the processing agreement. Relationship among joint controllers Joint controllers shall in a transparent manner determine and agree on their respective responsibilities for compliance with the obligations under the GDPR."

The rep resentative should act on behalf of the controller or the processor and may be addressed by any supervisory authority. The representative should be explicitly designated by a written mandate of the controller or of the processor to act on its behalf with regard to its obligations under this Regulation. The designation of such a rep resentative does not affect the responsibility or liability of the controller or of the processor under this Regulation. Such a representative should perform its tasks according to the mandate received from the controller or processor, including cooperating with the competent supervisory authorities with regard to any action taken to ensure compliance with this Regulation. The designated representative should be subject to enforcement proceedings in the event of non-compliance by the controller or processor. (81) To ensure compliance with the requirements of this Regulation in respect of the processing to be carried out by the processor on behalf of the controller, when entrusting a processor with processing activities, the controller should use only processors providing sufficient guarantees, in particular in terms of expert knowledge, reliability and resources, to implement technical and organisational measures which will meet the requirements of this Regulation, including for the security of processing. The adherence of the processor to an approved code of conduct or an approved certification mechanism may be used as an element to demonstrate compliance with the obligations of the controller. The carrying-out of processing by a processor should be governed by a contract or other legal act under Union or Member State law, binding the processor to the controller, setting out the subject- matter and duration of the processing, the nature and purposes of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects, taking into account the specific tasks and responsibilities of the processor in the context of the processing to be carried out and the risk to the rights and freedoms of the data subject. The controller and processor may choose to use an individual contract or standard contractual clauses which are adopted either directly by the Commission or by a supervisory authority in accordance with the consistency mechanism and then adopted by the Commission. After the completion of the processing on behalf of the controller, the processor should, at the choice of the controller, return or delete the personal data, unless there is a requirement to store the personal data under Union or Member State law to which the processor is subject. (82) In order to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation, the controller or processor should maintain records of processing activities under its responsibility. Each controller and processor should be obliged to cooperate with the supervisory authority and make those records, on request, available to it, so that it might serve for monitoring those processing operations. (83) In order to maintain security and to prevent processing in infringement of this Regulation, the controller or processor should evaluate the risks inherent in the processing and implement measures to mitigate those risks, such as encryption. ragPromptContext: [method] Processing Other Than By Automated Means — This refers to the processing of personal data manually, often as part of a filing system.

[concept] Processing — Processing, in the context of data management and privacy, encompasses any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data. These operations can be conducted through automated means or otherwise. This broad definition includes, but is not limited to, collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction. The concept of processing extends to any act of handling or dealing with data, directly or indirectly, that has the potential to affect the interests and fundamental rights of data subjects. For operations involving personal data, it is crucial to determine specific purposes and means, often requiring consent from the data subject. A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor. Infringements related to operations involving personal data can lead to liability, damage, and potential legal proceedings.
Any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation or alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction, as defined in Article 2(2) GDPR.

[method] Processing Operations — Processing Operations refer to any activities or a set of operations performed on data, particularly personal data, by institutions or data brokers. These operations encompass a vast array of actions, including the collection, storage, use, disclosure, further processing, the management of data subject rights, and the handling and manipulation of data. They can also involve linking data, forming different conducts, combining data, or cross-using data. Per Article 4(2) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), these operations are defined as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or on sets of personal data. These operations are composed of various components, such as data, systems, and processes, all of which should adhere to specific criteria. Activities often include the selection of targeting criteria and the display of advertisements to a specific target audience. Processing operations are a primary object of certification under the GDPR, potentially encompassing governance processes and leading to the creation of a product or service. Both data controllers and processors are obligated to demonstrate compliance when executing these operations. Actions performed on personal data should be limited to what is necessary, contributing to a defined processing purpose, and designed to process only the minimum amount of necessary data. Processing operations are actions carried out by a data controller using collected data, requiring specific information provisions and legal bases. They may also benefit from special regimes under GDPR. Examples include the collection, storage, use, or deletion of data. Some operations may involve the use of CCTV and are subject to the applicability of the household exemption. Records must be maintained for these data handling activities. Furthermore, processing operations that involve personal data may require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR if they pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. When a DPIA is required, these activities necessitate a systematic description, an assessment of necessity, proportionality, and risks, and the implementation of measures to address those risks.
Processing Operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction.
Processing Operations involve any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, etc.
Actions or sets of actions performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, or disclosure.
Actions or sets of actions performed upon personal data, which supervisory authorities are generally competent to oversee, except for courts acting in judicial capacity.
Processing operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, as defined in Article 4(2) GDPR.
Processing operations refer to activities involving personal data, such as combining or cross-using data.

[concept] Article 6(4) DMA — Article 6(4) of the DMA requires gatekeepers providing operating system core platform services to allow and technically enable the installation and effective use of third-party software applications or software application stores on their operating system.
This article pertains to the distribution of software application stores and applications, ensuring GDPR compliance.
Article 6(4) DMA outlines requirements for gatekeepers regarding the distribution of software application stores and software applications.
Article 6(4) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) outlines requirements for gatekeepers regarding third-party apps and app stores, including allowing installation, effective use, and enabling default settings, while also allowing for necessary and proportionate protective measures.
Article 6(4) of the DMA allows for certain measures to be put in place by gatekeepers, provided they do not undermine effective compliance.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[concept] Operating System — Software that needs to be kept up to date on various machines within a network as a security measure.
An operating system is a platform with which third-party apps or app stores may use or interoperate.
The core software that manages computer hardware and software resources, with which third-party apps and app stores must be allowed to interoperate.
An operating system is a fundamental software platform provided by gatekeepers that facilitates the functioning of hardware and applications.
A software system that manages computer hardware and software resources, within which gatekeepers allow access for apps and app stores.

[organization] Producers — Producers are entities that develop processing solutions (hardware, software, services, systems). They should demonstrate Data Protection by Design and Default (DPbDD) in their development life-cycle and facilitate controllers' needs.
Producers are key enablers for DPbDD, providing solutions to controllers that embed data protection.
Producers are responsible for developing, designing, selecting, and using applications, services, and products with regard to data protection.
[artifact] Optic-Electronic Devices — Optic-Electronic Devices are tools used for monitoring publicly accessible areas on a large scale.

[method] Targeted Technical and Organisational Measures — Targeted technical and organisational measures are efforts, possibly jointly with Article 6(4) DMA beneficiaries, to handle personal data breaches and restore data availability.

[organization] Online Social Network Operator — An online social network operator processes personal data, and such processing is subject to Article 9(1) and 9(2) GDPR.
An online social network operator processes personal data, and such processing is subject to Article 9(1) and 9(2) GDPR.
Under GDPR, Controller The controller must provide a way for human intervention in automated decisions. Human Intervention.

Under GDPR, Processing The processor performs the processing of personal data on behalf of the controller.<SEP>A processor is involved in the same processing concerning data.<SEP>A Processor is involved in Processing and can be liable for damage caused by it. Processor.
Under GDPR, Controller The controller must communicate any rectification of personal data. Rectification of Personal Data.
Under GDPR, Processing Operations Processing Operations Security is concerned with the protection of processing operations. Processing Operations Security.
Under GDPR, Article 6(4) DMA Article 6(4) of the DMA allows measures to impede software that disables or alters operating system functioning. Software.

Under GDPR, Controller A controller may choose to document breaches as part of its Record of Processing Activities.<SEP>Each controller shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility. Record of Processing Activities.

Under GDPR, Optic-Electronic Devices Processing of Personal Data for monitoring publicly accessible areas on a large scale often involves the use of optic-electronic devices. Processing of Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Controller The Controller should have appropriate technical measures in place to ensure personal data security.<SEP>The controller should have internal processes and technical measures to detect and address breaches.<SEP>The controller should implement technical measures appropriate for data protection. Technical Measures.

Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. This relationship mandates that the Controller select Processors who offer sufficient guarantees regarding GDPR compliance. This relationship is formalized and governed by a legally binding contract or other legal act, often referred to as a processing agreement. This agreement details how GDPR requirements will be implemented, outlines specific obligations, and defines assistance duties. The Controller must provide documented instructions to the Processor on how to process personal data, and the Processor is obligated to comply. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. This assistance includes deleting or returning personal data at the Controller's choice, providing compliance information, and cooperating with Controller-conducted audits. A critical obligation for the Processor is to notify the Controller "without undue delay" upon becoming aware of a personal data breach it is processing on behalf of the Controller, as mandated by Article 33(2) GDPR. Processors must also notify the Controller of any request from a third-country authority without undue delay and follow the Controller's instructions, unless prohibited by law. The Processor is liable to the Controller for fulfilling these obligations. The Controller can authorize the use of sub-processors, but the Processor must obtain prior written authorization from the Controller for engaging another processor. The Processor is liable to the Controller for the sub-processors' adherence to data protection obligations. In scenarios involving data transfers, such as a third-country company (Controller) engaging a non-EEA processor, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the Controller. The Controller must provide a comprehensive list of all data recipients, including processors. The relationship demands good faith cooperation, involving contract negotiation and management of audit and instruction processes. Controllers also carry out Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) with the processors. In some cases, the lead supervisory authority of the Controller may also become the lead supervisory authority for the Processor. When an end user qualifies as a Controller, an authorized third party may act as a Processor. Processor.
Under GDPR, Delivery Service Identification details may be cross-used by a delivery service without consent, under Article 5(2), point (c) DMA. Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Controller A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.<SEP>The controller decides on the purposes and means of processing personal data.<SEP>A controller is involved in the same processing concerning data.<SEP>Any Controller involved in Processing shall be liable for damage caused by Processing which infringes this Regulation. Processing.
Under GDPR, Producers Producers should be encouraged to take into account the right to data protection when developing products, services, and applications. Right to Data Protection.
Under GDPR, Processor Each processor shall maintain a record of all categories of processing activities carried out on behalf of a controller. Record of Processing Activities.
Under GDPR, Accredited Monitoring Body An Accredited Monitoring Body monitors Processor compliance and takes action in cases of infringement. Processor.
Under GDPR, Data Processing Equipment The Supervisory Authority can obtain access to data processing equipment. Supervisory Authority.
Under GDPR, Personal Data Breaches Targeted technical and organisational measures are for the effective handling of personal data breaches. Targeted Technical and Organisational Measures.

Under GDPR, Processor Processors must implement technical measures to meet the requirements of the Regulation, including for the security of processing.<SEP>The processor implements appropriate technical and organisational measures and assists the controller in ensuring compliance with security measures. Technical Measures.
Under GDPR, Controller Codes of conduct recommend dispute resolution procedures for resolving disputes between controllers and data subjects. Dispute Resolution Procedures.
Under GDPR, Business User A business user may access performance data for providing customer support. Performance Data.
Under GDPR, Gatekeeper Gatekeepers may need to take measures, alone or jointly with developers, to handle personal data breaches. Personal Data Breaches.

Under GDPR, GDPR The relationship between GDPR and a Processor is characterized by specific obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities directly imposed upon the Processor by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). A processor is subject to the GDPR for any given processing operation, with its role and duties explicitly defined within the regulation. This subjection is set forth in Article 3 of the GDPR, which establishes its territorial scope and applicability, even extending to non-EEA processors when they are engaged by third-country companies. In such cases, these processors must also comply with Article 28 and Chapter V of the GDPR. The GDPR directly imposes various obligations on processors, detailing their responsibilities concerning personal data protection. Processors must ensure compliance with these requirements, particularly by adhering to the instructions provided by controllers. Key responsibilities include compliance with Article 30 (records of processing activities), Article 32 (security of processing), Article 35 (data protection impact assessment), and Article 36 (prior consultation with a supervisory authority) regarding risks. Processors are also subject to GDPR obligations relating to their liability for sub-processors, as outlined in Article 28(4). Furthermore, the GDPR requires processors to implement appropriate security measures and outlines their obligations regarding data breaches and notifications, including the requirement to notify any breach to their controller. Supervisory Authorities (SAs) have the power to take action against a processor for infringing GDPR provisions. The regulation categorizes various infringements that can lead to fines for processors. Certifications under the GDPR are also issued to data processors, further emphasizing their direct accountability and the regulatory oversight they are subject to. These collective requirements define the responsibility and liability of the processor under the GDPR.<SEP>The GDPR, specifically Article 60(10), imposes duties on the processor.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for ensuring data processing adheres to GDPR provisions.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for compliance with the GDPR and must be able to demonstrate it.<SEP>The processing by a processor is governed by a contract or legal act that ensures compliance with GDPR articles. Processor.

Under GDPR, Controller If consent is withdrawn, the controller must stop processing operations based on that consent.<SEP>The controller is responsible for maintaining records of processing operations. Processing Operations.
Under GDPR, Auditor The processor must make information available and contribute to audits conducted by the auditor. Processor.
Under GDPR, Processing Activities The processor should maintain records of processing activities under its responsibility. Processor.
Under GDPR, Article 33 GDPR Targeted technical and organisational measures ensure compliance with Article 33 of the GDPR. Targeted Technical and Organisational Measures.
Under GDPR, Damage Processing that infringes this Regulation can cause Damage to a person. Processing.
Under GDPR, Gatekeeper Gatekeepers may have processors of personal data within their corporate structure. Processor.
Under GDPR, Personal Data Personal data can be processed for the purposes of planning and organisation of work. Planning and Organisation of Work.
Under GDPR, Board The secretariat of the Board provides translations for relevant information to the Board. Secretariat of the Board.
Under GDPR, Online Search Engine The third-party undertaking requesting access is often one providing an online search engine. Third-Party Undertaking Requesting Access.

Insofar as compliance with the GDPR is concerned, a controller is responsible, pursuant to Article 4(7), Article 5(2) and Article 24(1) of that Regulation, for the processing of personal data where it defines the means and purposes of such processing. 86 Recital 50 DMA. 87 Idem 92. Gatekeepers, as providers of operating systems, and app developers, should generally be considered as separate controllers under the GDPR since they define, independently of each other, the means and purposes of processing of personal data in relation to the respective operating system, app or app store. Article 6(4) DMA does not intend to establish any joint controllership or controller-processor relationship between a gatekeeper and an app developer as a beneficiary of that provision. 93. Gatekeepers should take account of the division of responsibility and liability between themselves and third parties providing apps and app stores, and ensure that they do not implement measures that would undermine or circumvent effective compliance with Article 6(4) of the DMA. Gatekeepers should pay particular attention to any technical or contractual measures they seek to impose which may be intended to prescribe the way a third party, such as an app developer, complies with the GDPR. In this regard, as a separate and independent controller, the third party remains responsible and liable for its own processing and should therefore be free to choose how it ensures that such processing complies with the GDPR. 3.1 Measures to ensure compliance with the GDPR principle of integrity and confidentiality in relation to personal data 94. Gatekeepers’ measures designed to safeguard the integrity of the gatekeeper’s hardware or operating system and/or applied to enable end users to protect their security from being undermined in accordance with Article 6(4) DMA are consistent with the gatekeepers’ obligation under Article 32 of the GDPR to ensure a level of security of personal data appropriate to the risk. 95. For example, Article 6(4) of the DMA allows measures to prevent the transmission of malicious code that may compromise an end user’s security or disrupt the functioning of the operating system or the hardware, or to impede software which disables or alters the normal functioning of the operating system or the hardware. Similarly, gatekeepers may enable end users to decide whether they allow beneficiaries under Article 6(4) of the DMA, such as third-party app and app store providers (“Article 6(4) DMA beneficiaries”), to gain access to certain sensitive information such as location, photos, or contacts. When doing so, gatekeepers may offer end users the possibility to limit access to such sensitive information (e.g., once, while using the app, or not to allow such access altogether) provided that gatekeepers also offer those possibilities to end users of their own services, and that they do not impose more restrictive measures on third-party app or app store providers than they apply to their own services. 96. In addition, measures such as requiring the encryption of network connections, which may not be strictly related to protecting the integrity of the device or its operating system, or to enabling end users to protect their security, may be necessary for the gatekeeper’s compliance with its obligations under Article 32 of the GDPR and therefore in line with Article 8(1) DMA. 97. Gatekeepers may also need to take additional appropriate measures, alone or jointly with developers of third-party apps or app stores, to comply with their obligations stemming from the GDPR, while ensuring that those measures do not contradict or unjustifiably frustrate the effective implementation of Article 6(4) of the DMA or other DMA provisions. Appropriate measures may, in particular, include targeted technical and organisational measures enabling the effective handling, alone or jointly with relevant Article 6(4) DMA beneficiaries, of personal data breaches to ensure compliance with Articles 33 and 34 of the GDPR. These targeted measures include, inter alia, the ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident and should be appropriate to comply with the GDPR and other legal requirements including, but not limited to, legal requirements stemming from the Cyber Resilience Act.88 98. There are some difficulties in interpretation as Recital 18 of Directive 2000/31/CE of the European Parliament and of the Council of June 8, 2000 provides a definition both broad and ambiguous of the notion of “the direct provision of information society services”. It mainly indicates that these services “span a wide range of economic activities which take place on-line”, but specifies that they are not restricted to “services giving rise to on-line contracting but also, in so far as they represent an economic activity, extend to services which are not remunerated by those who receive them, such as those offering on-line information or commercial communications, or those providing tools allowing for search, access and retrieval of data”, outlining the criteria of economic activity. 41. ragPromptContext: [person] Auditor — An auditor, who can be mandated by the controller, conducts inspections/audits to verify compliance.
[method] Inspections — Inspections are supervisory measures that can be requested as part of mutual assistance between supervisory authorities.

[organization] Certification Bodies — Certification Bodies are organizations that play a crucial role in establishing and maintaining certification mechanisms, particularly in the context of data protection. These entities are responsible for drafting, presenting, and revising the criteria used for the approval of various certification mechanisms. They possess appropriate data protection expertise and are tasked with performing certification activities. Furthermore, Certification Bodies are accredited to issue and renew certifications, ensuring that products, services, or systems meet specific requirements. They are often referred to as conformity assessment bodies. Under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), specifically Article 42(1) and Article 43, these organizations are subject to accreditation by supervisory authorities or national accreditation bodies. Their functions include determining data protection certification criteria and, in some instances, being responsible for accrediting data protection certification mechanisms and seals.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[concept] Monitoring, Inspection or Regulatory Function — This refers to a potential limitation under Article 23(2)(h) GDPR when connected to the exercise of official authority.
A ground for restriction related to official oversight activities.
Official activities connected to the exercise of official authority, which can be a ground for restricting data protection rights.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.
[concept] Structured Format — A way of organizing data that allows for easy extraction and analysis, a requirement for personal data portability.

[content] Standardized Icons — Standardized icons are a form of information for which the Commission can provide procedures.
Standardized icons are machine-readable visual representations used to provide a meaningful overview of intended data processing, combined with information from Articles 13 and 14.

[concept] Data Transfers — Data transfers involve the movement of data from one location or entity to another.
Data Transfers refer to the movement of data to third countries or international organizations, which can be based on appropriate safeguards and legal remedies for data subjects.
Data transfers involve the movement of personal data, and possible risks due to absence of adequacy decisions or safeguards (Article 46) must be informed.
Data Transfers involve the movement of personal data from one entity or location to another, especially across borders.
[concept] Secure Storage Space — A dedicated local storage space offered by gatekeepers to protect data from malware.

Therefore, the terms “data concerning health”, “processing for the purpose of scientific research” as well as “further processing” (also referred to as “primary and secondary usage of health data”) must be defined. 3.1 “Data concerning health” 7. According to Article 4 (15) GDPR, “data concerning health” means “personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of health care services, which reveal information about his or her health status”. As indicated by Recital 53, data concerning health deserves higher protection, as the use of such sensitive data may have significant adverse impacts for data subjects. In the light of this and the relevant jurisprudence of the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”),4 the term “data concerning health” must be given a wide interpretation. 8. Data concerning health can be derived from different sources, for example: 1. Information collected by a health care provider in a patient record (such as medical history and results of examinations and treatments). 2. Information that becomes health data by cross referencing with other data thus revealing the state of health or health risks (such as the assumption that a person has a higher risk of suffering heart attacks based on the high blood pressure measured over a certain period of time). 3. Information from a “self check” survey, where data subjects answer questions related to their health (such as stating symptoms). 4. Information that becomes health data because of its usage in a specific context (such as information regarding a recent trip to or presence in a region affected with COVID-19 processed by a medical professional to make a diagnosis). 3.2 “Processing for the purpose of scientific research” 9. Article 4 GDPR does not entail an explicit definition of “processing for the purpose of scientific research”. As indicated by Recital 159, “the term processing of personal data for scientific research purposes should be interpreted in a broad manner including for example technological development and demonstration, fundamental research, applied research and privately funded research. In addition, it should take into account the Union’s objective under Article 179 (1) TFEU of achieving a European Research Area. Scientific research purposes should also include studies conducted in the public interest in the area of public health.” 10. The former Article 29-Working-Party has already pointed out that the term may not be stretched beyond its common meaning though and understands that “scientific research” in this context means 4 See for example, regarding the Directive 95/46/EC, ECJ 6.11.2003, C-101/01 (Lindqvist) paragraph 50. Adopted 6 “a research project set up in accordance with relevant sector-related methodological and ethical standards, in conformity with good practice”.5 3.3 “Further processing” 11. Finally, when talking about “processing of health data for the purpose of scientific research”, there are two types of data usages: 1. Research on personal (health) data which consists in the use of data directly collected for the purpose of scientific studies (“primary use”). 2. Research on personal (health) data which consists of the further processing of data initially collected for another purpose (“secondary use”). 12. Example 1: For conducting a clinical trial on individuals suspected to be infected with SARS-CoV-2, health data are collected and questionnaires are used. This is a case of “primary use” of health data as defined above. 13. Example 2: A data subject has consulted a health care provider as a patient regarding symptoms of the SARS-CoV-2. If health data recorded by the health care provider is being used for scientific research purposes later on, this usage is classified as further processing of health data (secondary use) that has been collected for another initial purpose. 14. The distinction between scientific research based on primary or secondary usage of health data will become particularly important when talking about the legal basis for the processing, the information obligations and the purpose limitation principle pursuant to Article 5 (1) (b) GDPR as outlined below. 4 LEGAL BASIS FOR THE PROCESSING 15. All processing of personal data concerning health must comply with the principles relating to processing set out in Article 5 GDPR and with one of the legal grounds and the specific derogations listed respectively in Article 6 and Article 9 GDPR for the lawful processing of this special category of personal data.6 16. Legal bases and applicable derogations for processing health data for the purpose of scientific research are provided for respectively in Article 6 and Article 9. In the following section, the rules concerning consent and respective national legislation are addressed. It has to be noted that there is no ranking between the legal bases stipulated in the GDPR. 4.1 Consent 17. The consent of the data subject, collected pursuant to Article 6 (1) (a) and Article 9 (2) (a) GDPR, may provide a legal basis for the processing of data concerning health in the COVID-19 context. 18. However, it has to be noted that all the conditions for explicit consent, particularly those found in Article 4 (11), Article 6 (1) (a), Article 7 and Article 9 (2) (a) GDPR, must be fulfilled. [concept] Processing — Processing, in the context of data management and privacy, encompasses any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data. These operations can be conducted through automated means or otherwise. This broad definition includes, but is not limited to, collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction. The concept of processing extends to any act of handling or dealing with data, directly or indirectly, that has the potential to affect the interests and fundamental rights of data subjects. For operations involving personal data, it is crucial to determine specific purposes and means, often requiring consent from the data subject. A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor. Infringements related to operations involving personal data can lead to liability, damage, and potential legal proceedings.
Any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation or alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction, as defined in Article 2(2) GDPR.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[concept] Article 5(2) DMA — Article 5(2) DMA is a specific legal provision within the Digital Markets Act (DMA) that primarily addresses end-user choice and consent concerning the processing of personal data by gatekeepers. This article outlines prohibitions and conditions for gatekeepers regarding certain processing operations, explicitly stating that these cannot be carried out without the end users’ valid consent. It covers requirements for operations involving data processing and sign-in practices. The provision details legal obligations for gatekeepers concerning specific types of personal data processing that necessitate consent. These activities include processing personal data for online advertising, combining or cross-using personal data, and signing in end users. Article 5(2) DMA also sets requirements for consent requests, emphasizing clarity of presentation and limiting their repetition. It encompasses specific choice principles and the provision of less personalized alternatives to users, ensuring that gatekeepers adhere to stringent guidelines regarding end-user data privacy and consent within the digital marketplace. While its primary focus is on processing operations that require consent, Article 5(2) DMA also outlines certain processing operations that gatekeepers *may* engage in without end-user consent, provided they meet the requirements of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Overall, this article specifies requirements for gatekeepers related to combining or cross-using personal data, managing consent, and ensuring end-user choice in how their personal data is handled.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Lead Supervisory Authority is central to the oversight of cross-border data processing, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. In situations involving both a Controller and a Processor, the Lead Supervisory Authority for the Controller typically assumes the role for both, as outlined in Recital 36. Furthermore, the supervisory authority of a Member State where a Controller's main establishment is located often acts as the competent Lead Supervisory Authority. Beyond notification, the Lead Supervisory Authority serves as the sole interlocutor for the Controller regarding cross-border processing, meaning the Controller interacts exclusively with this authority. [person] Employee — An Employee is defined as an individual who is employed by an organization or person, belonging to the legal entity of a data controller or processor. These individuals are typically authorized to process personal data, acting under the authority of the controller. Their access to personal data should be restricted based on their specific duties and role within the company. Employees may interact with personal data in various ways, such as manually deleting personal data after its retention period in accordance with internal procedures. They can also be subjects whose personal data, such as their name, is processed by services (e.g., a taxi service in an illustrative example). Employee actions can also lead to incidents, such as when an employee of a controller makes a mistake resulting in a data breach, or when an employee of a service provider has their electronic notebook stolen, as depicted in CASE No. 11. While employees generally operate under established authority, there can be exceptional cases where they unlawfully exceed this authority. Furthermore, employees may face pressure concerning consent for data processing.
Employees are individuals within an organization who may have concerns or complaints.
An employee is a data subject who has a relevant and appropriate relationship with a controller, often forming the basis for legitimate interest in data processing within a group of undertakings.

[concept] Health Care Expenditure And Financing — Health Care Expenditure And Financing refers to the costs associated with healthcare and how these costs are covered.

[concept] Legal Claims — Legal Claims refer to the establishment, exercise, or defense of legal rights in a legal context. These claims represent demands for legal or equitable relief made by one party against another, or a formal demand for legal action or compensation. In this capacity, they can justify the lawful retention of personal data and may necessitate the processing of such data. The concept of Legal Claims is pertinent to data protection regulations, specifically appearing as a basis for data processing under GDPR Article 17.3.e. This article allows for an exception to delisting requests, enabling the continued use of personal data when necessary for the establishment, exercise, or defense of legal claims, though this exemption is considered unlikely to be frequently invoked by search engine providers. Furthermore, Legal Claims serve as a basis for data transfers under Article 49 (1) (e), encompassing various procedures including judicial, administrative, and out-of-court settings. This implies that the transfer of personal data may be necessary for establishing, exercising, or defending rights through legal action. Additionally, the establishment, exercise, or defense of rights in a legal context, through Legal Claims, can be a reason for processing restricted personal data.
The establishment, exercise, or defence of legal claims can justify the lawful retention of personal data.
Claims made in a court of law that require personal data for establishment, exercise, or defence.

Legal Claims refer to the establishment, exercise, or defense of rights through legal action, for which data transfer may be necessary.
[concept] Compensation — Compensation is the right for any person who has suffered damage due to an infringement of the Regulation to receive payment from the controller or processor.

[concept] Complaint — A Complaint is defined as a formal expression of grievance, grievance due to dissatisfaction, or dissatisfaction with an activity or service, such as the processing of personal data. These grievances are typically lodged with a supervisory authority, making it a Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA) particularly involved in the case. A complaint serves as the basis for investigations, specifically regarding data subjects' rights and alleged GDPR infringements, and defines the scope of data processing under scrutiny for potential violations. Upon receiving a complaint, the supervisory authority can take various actions, including dismissing, rejecting, or acting upon it. The granting of a complaint can be full or partial, and any decision made regarding it by supervisory authorities is considered an envisaged action. Furthermore, a complaint is considered a piece of relevant information that CSAs are obligated to proactively disclose to the Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) and other CSAs. The lodging of a complaint necessitates that a draft decision be submitted, especially when it leads to an investigation.
A complaint is a formal grievance lodged by a data subject, which may be rejected in whole or in part by a supervisory authority.
A formal statement of grievance lodged with a supervisory authority concerning a possible infringement of the Regulation.
