Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data Breach)" describes the responsibilities and actions of a data controller when a personal data breach occurs. The controller is tasked with detecting or becoming aware of such a breach, often through a security incident. Upon awareness, the controller must establish if a genuine personal data breach has taken place and then assess the associated risks to individuals. A primary responsibility of the controller is to address and mitigate the effects of the personal data breach. This includes documenting the breach, describing its nature, and implementing remedial actions. Furthermore, significant notification obligations are imposed on the controller under Article 33 following a personal data breach, requiring them to report the incident as stipulated. Overall, the controller is expected to recognize a personal data breach, take appropriate steps to manage it, and fulfill all regulatory requirements.<SEP>The controller should notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay.<SEP>The Controller is responsible for communicating a Personal Data Breach to the Data Subject if it poses a high risk.<SEP>The controller shall document any personal data breaches, including facts, effects, and remedial action. Personal Data Breach.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Supervisory Authority is established primarily by data protection regulations, such as the GDPR, and focuses on compliance, breach management, and accountability. A central obligation of the Controller is to notify the Supervisory Authority of personal data breaches, typically within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, especially if it poses a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, as per Article 33(1) and Article 27(5) GDPR. The Controller is responsible for determining if a breach is notifiable and must ensure the relevant Supervisory Authority is informed, potentially proactively notifying them of infringements or seeking advice. They must also inform the Supervisory Authority about data transfers, documenting assessments and safeguards. Controllers without an EU establishment are required to engage with local supervisory authorities in every Member State where they operate. Furthermore, the Controller must consult the Supervisory Authority if a high risk identified in a Data Protection Impact Assessment cannot be mitigated by reasonable means before processing. Controllers are also obligated to cooperate with and make records available to the Supervisory Authority upon request, demonstrating accountability and compliance. The Supervisory Authority plays a significant role in overseeing the Controller's data protection practices. It can advise Controllers on how to inform individuals about breaches and may even order them to do so, particularly for high-risk breaches. The Supervisory Authority verifies the Controller's compliance, handles complaints, and seeks amicable settlements regarding possible infringements. It possesses powers to require the Controller to provide information, carry out investigations, notify infringements, and obtain access to data and premises. The Supervisory Authority can issue warnings and reprimands, order compliance, and impose sanctions, including administrative fines under Article 83 GDPR, especially in cases of unjustified breaches. The level of the Controller's cooperation is considered by the Supervisory Authority when assessing mitigation efforts. The Supervisory Authority also promotes awareness among Controllers regarding their obligations under pertinent regulations and informs Controllers when a received complaint is dismissed or rejected. Supervisory Authority.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation between a Controller and a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is characterized by advisory support and assigned responsibility for data protection compliance, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Controller is responsible for designating a DPO to help ensure adherence to these regulations. The DPO's role encompasses providing advice and information to the Controller on various data protection matters, including breach management, data protection methodologies, and audits. This includes actively participating in Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), which the Controller undertakes with the DPO's guidance. Controllers are mandated to seek the DPO's advice when conducting a DPIA, and they must ensure the DPO's timely involvement in all data protection issues, providing necessary resources and access to facilitate their tasks. Guidelines may be developed by the Controller to specify when the DPO must be consulted. While the DPO offers crucial guidance and assists in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, the ultimate responsibility for data protection compliance remains with the Controller. The DPO may be an employee of the Controller or an external party, but they must perform their duties independently. The Controller is obligated to record the name and contact details of the DPO, and these details must be included in the record of processing activities. Furthermore, in the event of a data breach, the Controller must communicate the DPO's name and contact details as a contact point for breach information as part of the notification process. Data Protection Officer.

Under GDPR, Controller A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.<SEP>The controller decides on the purposes and means of processing personal data.<SEP>A controller is involved in the same processing concerning data.<SEP>Any Controller involved in Processing shall be liable for damage caused by Processing which infringes this Regulation. Processing.

Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. The GDPR recognizes that Controllers may not have all information immediately and allows for phased notification.<SEP>Controllers must comply with the provisions of the GDPR, including those related to information provision.<SEP>The controller must comply with GDPR requirements, including those related to transparency and notification.<SEP>A controller's responsibilities are defined under the GDPR. GDPR.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

Personal data needed to ensure interoperability can be separated in the following three major categories: a. the message content themselves that would be exchanged between servers of the gatekeeper and those of the other providers. b. the personal data that is needed to ensure technical aspects of interoperability between the NIICS of the gatekeeper and of the provider requesting interoperability, including to ensure that end users of the different NIICS can address each other and communicate. c. personal data that gatekeepers may process to ensure that the level of security they provide to their own end users is preserved across the interoperable services, in line with Article 7(3) DMA. 202. In relation to point b. in paragraph 201, gatekeepers need to decide how to resolve identities across the different NIICS. Users of a NIICS may obtain the identity of a user of another NIICS “out of band” (i.e. via a separate, independent communication channel, such as by email or verbally). Gatekeepers should then ensure that their end users have requested to use interoperable features from specific alternative NIICS before enabling end users of those NIICS to communicate with their end users. Furthermore, in light of Article 7(7) DMA, it is important that gatekeepers raise their end users’ awareness by informing them about the possibility to communicate across NIICS, including whenever a third party NIICS becomes interoperable with the gatekeeper’s NIICS. 203. In line with Article 7(7) DMA, end users of the gatekeepers’ NIICS and of the third party NIICS need to remain free to decide whether to make use of the interoperable basic functionalities that may be provided by the gatekeeper pursuant to Article 7(1) DMA. This means that end users should be free to decide whether to engage in conversations and be discoverable by users of third-party NIICS, including through automated discovery mechanisms that might entail the sharing of data that is not strictly required to ensure interoperability between the gatekeeper and the alternative NIICS provider where applicable. End users should remain free to opt-in to those mechanisms. 204. It is also relevant that the interoperability requests displayed to users specify the NIICS providers (i.e., the new controllers) that would gain access to some necessary end users’ personal data. If the number of providers of NIICS achieving interoperability becomes very significant, gatekeepers may want to avoid ‘choice fatigue’ by requesting end users to make their choices in parallel to “moments of discontinuity” in their relationship with end users (e.g. the moment of subscription, of a software update or during a communication campaign), or when the end user of an interoperable NIICS tries to initiate a communication. They may also implement simple interoperability management systems where end users can give, review, or modify their interoperability choices across multiple providers at once (while keeping the possibility to go granular if the user wishes to), thereby reducing repetitive requests. If end users accept the exchange of identity data between the gatekeepers and providers of other NIICS requesting interoperability, and the gatekeeper and the provider requesting interoperability establish a common naming convention, exchanging only the information defined in the convention (including the end user’s identifier in each of the NIICS) might be considered “strictly necessary” in accordance with Article 5(1), point (c) GDPR. 7.2 Personal data processing to preserve the level of security across interoperable services 205. Under Article 7(3) DMA, gatekeepers are required to preserve the level of security across interoperable services. In cases where the gatekeeper offers end-to-end- encryption to its end users of its NIICS, such encryption should be preserved across the interoperable services. End-to-end-encryption (“E2EE”) is generally understood as a technology that encrypts the content data on the end device of the sending party and decrypts it on the end device of the addressed recipient in such a way that only the sender and the recipient, at the exclusion of any third party, including the carrier or the chain of involved carriers, can access and control the content data of the communication.161 Maintaining trustworthy E2EE through the process of interoperability is key to ensure that the standard of security remains the same for end users in all services. 206. Ensuring E2EE across interoperable NIICS is a task that requires both the gatekeeper and the NIICS provider requesting interoperability to actively cooperate. In that context, the implemented libraries and software solution should be well defined. 207. From a data protection point of view, implementing a well-defined protocol for managing the exchange and certification of cryptographic keys between gatekeepers and providers of NIICS requesting interoperability would greatly contribute to a secure foundation for a reliable implementation of E2EE. From the perspective of the purpose limitation principle under Article 5(1), point (b) GDPR, gatekeepers should also consider appropriate measures to ensure that the different service providers can only use the keys as well as any other corresponding content exchanged for key agreement received from the gatekeeper for the intended purpose of enabling interoperability of the NIICS. 208. Another example of measures that gatekeepers should implement to maintain the level of security under Article 7(3) DMA having data protection implications are measures to protect the metadata of the communication between end users and use the minimum amount of metadata for effective encryption key management. Another possible measure is to cryptographically verify the authenticity of the communication"

The Hospital has also been identified as a victim of ransomware attacks (e.g., Case No. 03), where its information systems were compromised, leading to data encryption and subsequent delays in patient care. [organization] Commission — The Commission, most often referring to the European Commission, is a central body within the European Union with extensive responsibilities and powers, particularly in relation to data protection, digital markets, and legal frameworks. It serves as a regulatory authority with the sole power to implement and enforce the Digital Markets Act (DMA). The Commission issues guidelines, such as those in accordance with Article 47 DMA, and is solely responsible for interpreting the DMA provisions covered by these guidelines. It can impose sanctions, conduct proceedings and investigations under the DMA, and is involved in the coherent enforcement of both the DMA and GDPR, cooperating with national authorities and possessing investigatory powers. Under the GDPR, the Commission plays a crucial role in developing a code of icons for standardized information and is empowered to adopt delegated acts to determine the information for these icons. It can also adopt Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) to regulate data processing between controllers and processors and lay down such clauses more broadly. A key function includes making adequacy decisions regarding the level of data protection in third countries or international organizations for international data transfers. The Commission monitors these decisions, consults with the European Data Protection Board ("the Board" or EDPB), evaluates their functioning, and reports findings. It can also adopt delegated acts specifying criteria and requirements for certification mechanisms and standardized icons, and implementing acts for specifying technical standards for data protection certification and safeguards. It cooperates with supervisory authorities in third countries to develop international cooperation mechanisms regarding personal data protection, specifying formats and procedures for information exchange relating to Binding Corporate Rules and mutual assistance. Member States must notify the Commission of adopted laws and amendments related to data protection provisions, and the Commission receives Supervisory Authority activity reports. The Commission designates gatekeepers regarding Core Platform Services (CPSs) and recognizes adequacy for data transfers. It has legal powers to regulate data sharing under Article 6(11) DMA via an implementing act pursuant to Article 8(2) DMA. It may specify the ineligibility of potential third-party recipients and consult with other bodies to ensure compliance with DMA obligations. The Commission assesses whether a third country provides an adequate level of protection for personal data and sometimes considers the display of advertisements as part of online advertising CPS and other CPS. It receives audited descriptions of profiling techniques from gatekeepers and transmits them to the EDPB. The Commission participates in the Board's activities without voting rights, can designate a representative, and can request matters to be handled within the consistency mechanism, including requesting opinions from the Board. It is informed of Board decisions and receives communications from the Board Chair. Ultimately, the Commission is granted delegated power to adopt and notify delegated acts, prepare and submit reports, examine the application and functioning of the Regulation, request information, and submit proposals for the overall effectiveness and implementation of data protection regulations, cooperating with the EDPB and supervisory authorities to assess processing operations and consider guidelines for gatekeepers regarding interoperability and geographical limitations.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

ragPromptContext: [data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[concept] Medical Diagnosis — The process of identifying a disease or condition, which often involves the processing of personal data.

[organization] Hospital — A Hospital is a healthcare institution responsible for collecting and managing significant quantities of sensitive patient data, often utilizing an electronic health record system. This organization has been noted for experiencing a personal data breach where staff members could view unauthorized patient health files due to issues with authorization monitoring, specifically concerning staff retaining access to patient files after transferring departments; an internal investigation was conducted to address this. The sensitive nature of the data processed means that data breaches at a Hospital are highly impactful, and the unavailability of critical medical data can pose a substantial risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. Furthermore, a Hospital can also be an organization involved in scientific research, as exemplified by "Project X," which necessitates the use of real patient dental records. The Hospital has also been identified as a victim of ransomware attacks (e.g., Case No. 03), where its information systems were compromised, leading to data encryption and subsequent delays in patient care. Consequently, a Hospital is an organization legally obliged to notify relevant authorities and affected individuals in cases of cyber-attacks impacting medical records.

[person] M. Schulz — M. Schulz is identified as "The President" for the European Parliament at the time the Regulation was done.

[content] Processing Activities Record — A processing activities record is a document that each joint controller is required to maintain, detailing their data processing operations.

[concept] Processing — Processing, in the context of data management and privacy, encompasses any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data. These operations can be conducted through automated means or otherwise. This broad definition includes, but is not limited to, collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction. The concept of processing extends to any act of handling or dealing with data, directly or indirectly, that has the potential to affect the interests and fundamental rights of data subjects. For operations involving personal data, it is crucial to determine specific purposes and means, often requiring consent from the data subject. A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor. Infringements related to operations involving personal data can lead to liability, damage, and potential legal proceedings.
Any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation or alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction, as defined in Article 2(2) GDPR.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

[Source: edpb_guidelines_042022_calculationofadministrativefines_en] ". However, as it turned out, there were issues concerning the monitoring of authorisations. Staff members that transferred between departments were still able to gain access to the patient files from their “old” departments and the hospital had no procedures in place to match the current position of the staff member with their authorisation. Internal investigation by the hospital showed that at least 150 staff members (out of the 3500) had inaccurate authorisations, affecting at least 20,000 of the 95,000 patient files. The hospital could show that in at least 16 instances staff members had used their authorisations to view patient files. The supervisory authority considers that there has been a breach of Article 32 GDPR. In assessing the seriousness of the case, the supervisory authority first noted that an infringement of Article 32 GDPR is listed among the infringements of Article 83(4) GDPR and therefore falls within the lower tier of Article 83 GDPR. Secondly, the supervisory authority assessed the circumstances of the case. In that regard, the supervisory authority considered that even though the number of data subjects affected by the breach was only 16, this could potentially have been 20,000 in the circumstances of the case and even 95,000 given the systemic nature of the issue. Furthermore, the supervisory authority categorised the infringement as negligent, but to a low degree, which was considered a neutral factor in the circumstances of this particular case due to the fact that the hospital failed to adopt authorisation policies where it surely should have done so but had, otherwise, taken steps to implement strict measures to restrict access. This evaluation was not impacted by the fact that other data protection and security policies were implemented successfully, as the GDPR requires. Lastly, the supervisory authority attributed significant weight to the fact that the patient files include health data, which are special categories of data according to Article 9 GDPR. 23 Adopted Taking all the above into account (nature of the processing and special categories of data vis-à-vis the number of data subjects actually and potentially affected, the supervisory authority concludes that the infringement is considered to be at a medium level of seriousness. The supervisory authority will determine the starting amount for further calculation at a point between 10 and 20% of the legal maximum included in Article 83(4) GDPR. Example 5c – Qualifying the seriousness of an infringement (low level of seriousness) A supervisory authority has received numerous complaints about the way in which an online store handles the right of access of its data subjects. According to the complainants, the handling of their access requests has taken between 4 and 6 months, which is outside the timeframe permitted by the GDPR. The supervisory authority investigates the complaints and finds that the online store responds to access requests a maximum of three months too late in 5% of the cases. In total the store received around 1,000 access requests on an annual basis and confirmed that 950 of these were handled on time. Moreover, the online store had policies in place to safeguard that all access requests were handled correctly and fully. Nevertheless, the supervisory authority concluded that the online store infringed Article 12(3) GDPR and decided to impose a fine. During the calculation of the amount of the fine to be imposed, the supervisory authority was tasked with assessing the seriousness of this case. As a starting point, the supervisory authority noted that an infringement of Article 12 GDPR is listed among the infringements of Article 83(5) GDPR and therefore falls within the higher tier of Article 83 GDPR. Secondly, the supervisory authority assessed the circumstances of the case. In that regard, the supervisory authority carefully analysed the nature of the infringement. Even though the timely right to access to personal data is one of the cornerstones of the data subject rights, the supervisory authority considered that the infringement was of limited seriousness in this respect, given that all requests were handled eventually and with a limited delay. Considering the purpose of the processing, the supervisory authority found that the processing of personal data was not the core activity of the online store, but still an important ancillary in fulfilling its objective of selling goods online. The supervisory authority considered this to increase the seriousness of the infringement. On the other hand, the level of damage suffered by the data subjects was considered minimal, as all access requests were handled within 6 months. Taking all the above into account (nature of the infringement, purpose of the processing and level of damage), the supervisory authority concludes that the infringement is considered to be at a low level of seriousness. The supervisory authority will determine the starting amount for further calculation at a point between 0 and 10% of the legal maximum included in Article 83(5) GDPR. 4.3 - Turnover of the undertaking with a view to imposing an effective, dissuasive and proportionate fine 63. The GDPR requires each supervisory authority to ensure that the imposition of administrative fines is effective, proportionate and dissuasive in each individual case (Article 83(1) GDPR). The application of these principles of European Union law can have far-reaching consequences in individual cases, as the starting points that the GDPR offers for calculating administrative fines apply to micro-enterprises and multinational corporations alike. [person] Data Protection Officer — A Data Protection Officer (DPO) is an individual, organization, or team responsible for overseeing, advising on, and monitoring an entity's data protection strategy and its implementation to ensure compliance with relevant data protection laws and regulations, particularly the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), as detailed in Articles 37 to 39. This role requires expert knowledge of data protection law and practices. The DPO's responsibilities include providing guidance on appropriate measures and demonstrating compliance regarding personal data processing, assisting the controller or processor in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, and advising on Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), including their performance, monitoring, and documenting related advice and decisions. DPOs also play a crucial role in assessing the applicability of GDPR Article 6(1)(f). They act as a key contact point for information regarding personal data breaches, cooperating with supervisory authorities, and their contact details may need to be communicated as part of GDPR information duties. They are involved in all issues related to personal data protection, supported by controllers and processors with necessary resources, and report directly to the highest management level. Appointment of a DPO may be mandatory under GDPR Article 37, especially when an organization's core activities involve processing special categories of data or regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects, though organizations can also voluntarily appoint one. Whether an employee or an external contractor, the DPO must perform duties independently, without fear of dismissal or penalization, and avoid conflicts of interest, meaning they cannot represent a controller or processor in court for data protection matters. While responsible for monitoring compliance of data processing operations, the DPO's role cannot be certified under GDPR Article 42.7. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) encourages DPO involvement in integrating data protection by design and by default principles, highlighting their essential role in accountability and record-keeping in personal data protection.

[concept] Processing of Personal Data — Processing of Personal Data is defined as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or on sets of personal data. This comprehensive definition encompasses a wide array of activities, including the collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction of such data. It specifically refers to the handling or manipulation of information pertaining to an identified or identifiable natural person, whether or not by automated means, and also includes manual processing within a filing system. The processing of personal data is actively governed by various data protection rules and legal frameworks, most notably the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and PSD2 regulations. Article 5 of the GDPR outlines key principles that must be adhered to during such processing, emphasizing that operations must be lawful, fair, and transparent. The legality of these operations is established through specific legal bases, as detailed in Article 6(1)(b) of the GDPR, with consent being one of these permissible lawful bases. Operations involving personal data must be carried out lawfully, securely, and confidentially, safeguarding individuals' rights in compliance with these regulations. Furthermore, the processing of personal data is an activity for which a "controller" determines the purposes and means. It can be performed by various entities, and is central to discussions of concepts like joint controllership. This activity is also central to discussions about "core activities" and "large scale" operations under GDPR, especially when dealing with special categories of personal data, biometric data, or data on criminal convictions and offenses. The global relevance of this definition is underscored by calls for its inclusion in international agreements.
The handling or manipulation of personal data.

Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. The GDPR recognizes that Controllers may not have all information immediately and allows for phased notification.<SEP>Controllers must comply with the provisions of the GDPR, including those related to information provision.<SEP>The controller must comply with GDPR requirements, including those related to transparency and notification.<SEP>A controller's responsibilities are defined under the GDPR. Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

[organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.
[data] Business Performance Data — Data relating to the performance of a business user, which is within the scope of Article 6(10) DMA for data access.
[concept] Granularity and Duration of Portability — Refers to the level of detail and the time frame for which data portability is available.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.
[data] Employees' Personal Data — Employees' personal data refers to information about employees that is subject to specific rules and safeguards regarding its processing in the employment context.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation between a Controller and a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is characterized by advisory support and assigned responsibility for data protection compliance, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Controller is responsible for designating a DPO to help ensure adherence to these regulations. The DPO's role encompasses providing advice and information to the Controller on various data protection matters, including breach management, data protection methodologies, and audits. This includes actively participating in Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), which the Controller undertakes with the DPO's guidance. Controllers are mandated to seek the DPO's advice when conducting a DPIA, and they must ensure the DPO's timely involvement in all data protection issues, providing necessary resources and access to facilitate their tasks. Guidelines may be developed by the Controller to specify when the DPO must be consulted. While the DPO offers crucial guidance and assists in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, the ultimate responsibility for data protection compliance remains with the Controller. The DPO may be an employee of the Controller or an external party, but they must perform their duties independently. The Controller is obligated to record the name and contact details of the DPO, and these details must be included in the record of processing activities. Furthermore, in the event of a data breach, the Controller must communicate the DPO's name and contact details as a contact point for breach information as part of the notification process. Data Protection Officer.

Under GDPR, Automated Decision-Making The controller must inform about the use of data for automated decision-making where relevant.<SEP>Controllers are subject to Article 22 provisions if they use a profile in a solely automated decision-making process with significant effects.<SEP>The controller uses and regularly tests automated decision-making methods. Under GDPR, Personal Data The relation "(Personal Data, Processor)" defines the role and responsibilities of a Processor in handling Personal Data. A Processor is an entity that processes personal data strictly on behalf of and under the instructions of a Controller, operating as an agent in managing, extracting, handling, and transferring this data. Key duties include the implementation of robust security measures to protect the personal data entrusted to them. Processors are authorized to perform operations involving personal data, and individuals working under the direct authority of the Processor are also permitted to process such data. Upon the termination of processing activities, the Processor is generally obligated to either delete or return the personal data to the Controller, unless a legal requirement necessitates its storage. Furthermore, a Processor may transfer personal data, and within the context of the EU, they might even make personal data accessible to a third-country authority. Processor.

Under GDPR, GDPR Legal frameworks of a third country may impact a controller's ability to respect the GDPR.<SEP>GDPR mandates that processing activities in third countries address increased risks for lawfulness. Third Country.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation `(Controller, Processing of Personal Data)` describes the multifaceted role and responsibilities of a controller concerning the processing of personal data. A controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This determination is made independently, and the specified purposes and means must explicitly relate to the processing of personal data. In this context, the controller is actively involved in and carries out the processing of personal data. A core responsibility of the controller is to ensure and demonstrate compliance with the principles governing personal data processing, particularly those outlined in the GDPR. This includes ensuring that all processing activities have an appropriate legal basis. Furthermore, controllers are expected to innovate to maintain compliance with evolving legal parameters. The controller's responsibilities also extend to respecting the rights of data subjects. Specifically, if a data subject objects to the processing of their personal data, the controller shall cease processing unless compelling legitimate grounds for the processing can be demonstrated. Processing of Personal Data.

(68) To further strengthen the control over his or her own data, where the processing of personal data is carried out by automated means, the data subject should also be allowed to receive personal data concerning him or her which he or she has provided to a controller in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable and interoperable format, and to transmit it to another controller. Data controllers should be encouraged to develop interoperable formats that enable data portability. That right should apply where the data subject provided the personal data on the basis of his or her consent or the processing is necessary for the performance of a contract. It should not apply where processing is based on a legal ground other than consent or contract. By its very nature, that right should not be exercised against controllers processing personal data in the exercise of their public duties. It should therefore not apply where the processing of the personal data is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject or for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of an official authority vested in the controller. The data subject's right to transmit or receive personal data concerning him or her should not create an obligation for the controllers to adopt or maintain processing systems which are technically compatible. Where, in a certain set of personal data, more than one data subject is concerned, the right to receive the personal data should be without prejudice to the rights and freedoms of other data subjects in accordance with this Regulation. Furthermore, that right should not prejudice the right of the data subject to obtain the erasure of personal data and the limitations of that right as set out in this Regulation and should, in particular, not imply the erasure of personal data concerning the data subject which have been provided by him or her for the performance of a contract to the extent that and for as long as the personal data are necessary for the performance of that contract. Where technically feasible, the data subject should have the right to have the personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another. (69) Where personal data might lawfully be processed because processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller, or on grounds of the legitimate interests of a controller or a third party, a data subject should, nevertheless, be entitled to object to the processing of any personal data relating to his or her particular situation. It should be for the controller to demonstrate that its compelling legitimate interest overrides the interests or the fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject. (70) Where personal data are processed for the purposes of direct marketing, the data subject should have the right to object to such processing, including profiling to the extent that it is related to such direct marketing, whether with regard to initial or further processing, at any time and free of charge. That right should be explicitly brought to the attention of the data subject and presented clearly and separately from any other information. 4.5.2016 L 119/13 Official Journal of the European Union EN (71) The data subject should have the right not to be subject to a decision, which may include a measure, evaluating personal aspects relating to him or her which is based solely on automated processing and which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her, such as automatic refusal of an online credit application or e-recruiting practices without any human intervention. Such processing includes ‘profiling’ that consists of any form of automated processing of personal data evaluating the personal aspects relating to a natural person, in particular to analyse or predict aspects concerning the data subject's performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences or interests, reliability or behaviour, location or movements, where it produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her. However, decision-making based on such processing, including profiling, should be allowed where expressly authorised by Union or Member State law to which the controller is subject, including for fraud and tax-evasion monitoring and prevention purposes conducted in accordance with the regulations, standards and recommendations of Union institutions or national oversight bodies and to ensure the security and reliability of a service provided by the controller, or necessary for the entering or performance of a contract between the data subject and a controller, or when the data subject has given his or her explicit consent. In any case, such processing should be subject to suitable safeguards, which should include specific information to the data subject and the right to obtain human intervention, to express his or her point of view, to obtain an explanation of the decision reached after such assessment and to challenge the decision. Such measure should not concern a child. In order to ensure fair and transparent processing in respect of the data subject, taking into account the specific circumstances and context in which the personal data are processed, the controller should use appropriate mathematical or statistical procedures for the profiling, implement technical and organisational measures appropriate to ensure, in particular, that factors which result in inaccuracies in personal data are corrected and the risk of errors is minimised, secure personal data in a manner that takes account of the potential risks involved for the interests and rights of the data subject and that prevents, inter alia, discriminatory effects on natural persons on the basis of racial or ethnic origin, political opinion, religion or beliefs, trade union membership, genetic or health status or sexual orientation, or that result in measures having such an effect. Automated decision-making and profiling based on special categories of personal data should be allowed only under specific conditions. (72)"

[Source: joint_com-edpb_gls_interplay_dma_gdpr_for_public_consultation_en] "Article 6(10) DMA does not cover data that gatekeepers create on the basis of the data provided by the end user and/or observed based on the end user’s activities on the CPS (i.e., derived or inferred data). To comply with the data minimisation principle under Article 5(1), point (c) GDPR, the gatekeeper only has to make available to the requesting business user or authorised third party personal data of end users that is covered by the scope of Article 6(10) DMA. 151. When access to personal data is deemed relevant by business users, and at their request, gatekeepers should only enable the sharing of personal data if the end users whose personal data is requested have opted-in to such sharing by giving their consent within the meaning of the GDPR.124 152. The data access right in Article 6(10) DMA additionally applies to both aggregated and non-aggregated data. Gatekeepers will have to provide business users, and third parties authorised by business users, with aggregated data that is provided or generated in the context of the use of a relevant CPS, or services provided together with, or in support, of such relevant CPSs. On their end, pursuant to their own obligation under Article 5(1), point (c) GDPR, business users should consider whether the personal data that they request under Article 6(10) DMA is adequate and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they will process them (which is not for the gatekeeper to assess before giving access to the data). 153. Gatekeepers will also be required to provide access to data falling within the scope of Article 6(10) DMA that is exclusively processed on a device.125 To ensure compliance with Article 6(10) DMA, gatekeepers should enable effective, high-quality, continuous and real-time access to on-device data at the request of business users or their authorised third parties. Where personal data is concerned, and in line with the GDPR principles of data minimisation and purpose limitation, enabling business user or authorised third party access to such data under Article 6(10) DMA should not result in further access to on-device data by a gatekeeper itself. 154. In the context of their obligation to ensure and demonstrate compliance with Article 6(10) DMA, gatekeepers are encouraged to keep a record of all categories of data, including personal data, that are provided or generated by business users and end users of business users, in the context of the use of each designated CPS and where relevant, additional services of the gatekeeper, including those provided together with or in support of the relevant CPS.126 124 See Article 2(32) DMA: “‘consent means consent as defined in Article 4, point (11), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679” and Article 6(1), point (a) GDPR. 125 Data that has been provided or generated in the context of digital services is increasingly being processed and stored on the devices of users. This development is particularly driven by the use of new processing technologies, such as artificial intelligence. 126 Such a record is without prejudice to the record-keeping obligations of gatekeepers pursuant to Article 30 GDPR. 5.3 Granularity of data access under Article 6(10) DMA 155. Gatekeepers should ensure that requesting business users and their authorised third parties have clarity and control over the precise datasets that they wish to access and make use of, including end user personal data that is directly connected with the use of products or services offered by the relevant business user through the relevant CPS and services provided together with, or in support of, the relevant CPS. 156. At the same time, gatekeepers have to comply with the transparency principle of the GDPR and related transparency obligations before they process personal data access requests by business users or third parties authorised by business users.127 Gatekeepers should inform end users, through the relevant CPS privacy policies, about the right of business users and third parties under Article 6(10) DMA to request such access to the end user’s personal data, subject to the end user’s consent. In addition, gatekeepers should inform end users about specific recipients of their personal data pursuant to Article 6(10) DMA via a dedicated dashboard128 (a link to which may be included in the CPS’s privacy policy). This is particularly important given that the interface where end users consent to provide access to a business user, or a third party authorised by the business user, will generally be offered by the gatekeeper and not the business user. 157. Data access should be enabled for any business user data and end user data that is within scope of the obligation laid down in Article 6(10) DMA.
