(8) Where this Regulation provides for specifications or restrictions of its rules by Member State law, Member States may, as far as necessary for coherence and for making the national provisions comprehensible to the persons to whom they apply, incorporate elements of this Regulation into their national law. (9) The objectives and principles of Directive 95/46/EC remain sound, but it has not prevented fragmentation in the implementation of data protection across the Union, legal uncertainty or a widespread public perception that there are significant risks to the protection of natural persons, in particular with regard to online activity. Differences in the level of protection of the rights and freedoms of natural persons, in particular the right to the protection of personal data, with regard to the processing of personal data in the Member States may prevent the free flow of personal data throughout the Union. Those differences may therefore constitute an obstacle to the pursuit of economic activities at the level of the Union, distort competition and impede authorities in the discharge of their responsibilities under Union law. Such a difference in levels of protection is due to the existence of differences in the implementation and application of Directive 95/46/EC. (10) In order to ensure a consistent and high level of protection of natural persons and to remove the obstacles to flows of personal data within the Union, the level of protection of the rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of such data should be equivalent in all Member States. Consistent and homogenous application of the rules for the protection of the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data should be ensured throughout the Union. Regarding the processing of personal data for compliance with a legal obligation, for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller, Member States should be allowed to maintain or introduce national provisions to further specify the application of the rules of this Regulation. In conjunction with the general and horizontal law on data protection implementing Directive 95/46/EC, Member States have several sector-specific laws in areas that need more specific provisions. This Regulation also provides a margin of manoeuvre for Member States to specify its rules, including for the processing of special categories of personal data (‘sensitive data’). To that extent, this Regulation does not exclude Member State law that sets out the circumstances for specific processing situations, including determining more precisely the conditions under which the processing of personal data is lawful. 4.5.2016 L 119/2 Official Journal of the European Union EN (11) Effective protection of personal data throughout the Union requires the strengthening and setting out in detail of the rights of data subjects and the obligations of those who process and determine the processing of personal data, as well as equivalent powers for monitoring and ensuring compliance with the rules for the protection of personal data and equivalent sanctions for infringements in the Member States. (12) Article 16(2) TFEU mandates the European Parliament and the Council to lay down the rules relating to the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and the rules relating to the free movement of personal data. (13) In order to ensure a consistent level of protection for natural persons throughout the Union and to prevent divergences hampering the free movement of personal data within the internal market, a Regulation is necessary to provide legal certainty and transparency for economic operators, including micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, and to provide natural persons in all Member States with the same level of legally enforceable rights and obligations and responsibilities for controllers and processors, to ensure consistent monitoring of the processing of personal data, and equivalent sanctions in all Member States as well as effective cooperation between the supervisory authorities of different Member States. The proper functioning of the internal market requires that the free movement of personal data within the Union is not restricted or prohibited for reasons connected with the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data. To take account of the specific situation of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, this Regulation includes a derogation for organisations with fewer than 250 employees with regard to record-keeping. In addition, the Union institutions and bodies, and Member States and their supervisory authorities, are encouraged to take account of the specific needs of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises in the application of this Regulation. The notion of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises should draw from Article 2 of the Annex to Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC (1). (14) The protection afforded by this Regulation should apply to natural persons, whatever their nationality or place of residence, in relation to the processing of their personal data. This Regulation does not cover the processing of personal data which concerns legal persons and in particular undertakings established as legal persons, including the name and the form of the legal person and the contact details of the legal person. (15) In order to prevent creating a serious risk of circumvention, the protection of natural persons should be technolo gically neutral and should not depend on the techniques used. The protection of natural persons should apply to the processing of personal data by automated means, as well as to manual processing, if the personal data are contained or are intended to be contained in a filing system. Files or sets of files, as well as their cover pages, which are not structured according to specific criteria should not fall within the scope of this Regulation. [data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

ragPromptContext: [organization] Committee — The Committee assists the Commission and operates within the meaning of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011.
[organization] Secretariat of the Board — The Secretariat of the Board provides translations of relevant information as necessary.

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[concept] Accreditation Criteria — The standards and conditions a body must meet to be accredited to monitor codes of conduct.
Criteria for accreditation of bodies, approval of which requires an opinion from the Board as per Article 41(3) or Article 43(3).

[person] European Data Protection Supervisor — The European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) is an authority with a prominent role in data protection within the European Union. The EDPS is a member of the European Data Protection Board, holding specific voting rights concerning principles and rules applicable to Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, as outlined in Article 65 of relevant regulations. In this capacity, the EDPS also provides secretarial assistance to the Board and has the prerogative to establish a Memorandum of Understanding with it. The EDPS actively contributes to discussions on data protection by issuing opinions on various critical topics. For instance, the EDPS has published opinions on online manipulation and on the challenges posed by big data, including Opinion 7/2015 on big data released in November 2015. Additionally, the EDPS developed a toolkit to assist in assessing the necessity of measures that may limit personal data protection, which is also associated with Giovanni Buttarelli. The EDPS has also been consulted for specific regulations, providing an opinion on March 7, 2012, related to such regulatory frameworks.
[concept] Two Weeks — Two Weeks is the period within which the Board shall adopt a decision if unable to do so within the initial two months, or for urgent opinions/decisions.
[organization] Union (European Union) — The Union refers to the European Union, which has an important public interest.

[method] Data Protection Training — Appropriate training provided to personnel who have permanent or regular access to personal data to ensure their understanding and adherence to data protection principles.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[organization] Secretariat — The Secretariat is an administrative body that supports the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and undertakes several key functions, particularly in processing information and managing documentation. This entity reviews and analyzes the completeness of files, often on behalf of the Chair, and may request additional information from the Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) and/or Concerned Supervisory Authorities (CSAs) to remedy any omissions, especially when a binding decision is sought. The Secretariat is also responsible for evaluating redaction requirements, ensuring the right to be heard is afforded, and being informed of national decision notifications. Its duties further extend to translating documents into English, verifying objections, and referring matters to the EDPB. The Secretariat processes matters submitted to the EDPB, including those received from the LSA, and is involved in the procedure outlined in Article 11(2)(f) of the Rules of Procedure (RoP). Additionally, it performs notifications on behalf of the Chair.
The Secretariat assists the Board in its operations.
The Secretariat provides analytical, administrative, and logistical support to the Board and performs tasks exclusively under the instructions of the Board's Chair. It is provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor.

Under GDPR, Consent Consent, in the context of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), is a fundamental concept for lawful processing of personal data. The GDPR defines consent and establishes it as one of the six lawful bases for processing personal data, explicitly listed in Article 6. It also sets forth specific conditions and requirements for valid consent, notably in Article 7, with Article 4(11) providing a crucial definitional baseline. The legal framework of the GDPR governs the validity of consent, playing a significant role in assessing whether consent is freely given, particularly as outlined in Article 7(4) and Recital 43. This framework includes stricter standards for how consent must be obtained and managed, requiring controllers to ensure their consent mechanisms are fully compliant with GDPR provisions. For specific types of sensitive data, such as biometric data, processing requires consent that adheres to the stricter requirements of Article 9(2)(a) GDPR. Furthermore, the notion of consent within the ePrivacy Directive is interpreted in light of the GDPR, aligning with the consent requirements provided by Articles 4(11) and 7 of the GDPR. This emphasizes that for data processing activities, particularly those involving cookies and similar technologies under the ePrivacy Directive, GDPR guidelines for consent must be followed to ensure legality and adherence to an internationally recognized privacy standard.<SEP>Consent is defined and regulated under the GDPR as one of the legal grounds for processing personal data.<SEP>The GDPR provides the legal definition of "consent" for data subjects. [concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[organization] Secretariat — The Secretariat is an administrative body that supports the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and undertakes several key functions, particularly in processing information and managing documentation. This entity reviews and analyzes the completeness of files, often on behalf of the Chair, and may request additional information from the Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) and/or Concerned Supervisory Authorities (CSAs) to remedy any omissions, especially when a binding decision is sought. The Secretariat is also responsible for evaluating redaction requirements, ensuring the right to be heard is afforded, and being informed of national decision notifications. Its duties further extend to translating documents into English, verifying objections, and referring matters to the EDPB. The Secretariat processes matters submitted to the EDPB, including those received from the LSA, and is involved in the procedure outlined in Article 11(2)(f) of the Rules of Procedure (RoP). Additionally, it performs notifications on behalf of the Chair.
The Secretariat assists the Board in its operations.
The Secretariat provides analytical, administrative, and logistical support to the Board and performs tasks exclusively under the instructions of the Board's Chair. It is provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor.

[concept] Accreditation Criteria — The standards and conditions a body must meet to be accredited to monitor codes of conduct.
Criteria for accreditation of bodies, approval of which requires an opinion from the Board as per Article 41(3) or Article 43(3).

[organization] Commission — The Commission, most often referring to the European Commission, is a central body within the European Union with extensive responsibilities and powers, particularly in relation to data protection, digital markets, and legal frameworks. It serves as a regulatory authority with the sole power to implement and enforce the Digital Markets Act (DMA). The Commission issues guidelines, such as those in accordance with Article 47 DMA, and is solely responsible for interpreting the DMA provisions covered by these guidelines. It can impose sanctions, conduct proceedings and investigations under the DMA, and is involved in the coherent enforcement of both the DMA and GDPR, cooperating with national authorities and possessing investigatory powers. Under the GDPR, the Commission plays a crucial role in developing a code of icons for standardized information and is empowered to adopt delegated acts to determine the information for these icons. It can also adopt Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) to regulate data processing between controllers and processors and lay down such clauses more broadly. A key function includes making adequacy decisions regarding the level of data protection in third countries or international organizations for international data transfers. The Commission monitors these decisions, consults with the European Data Protection Board ("the Board" or EDPB), evaluates their functioning, and reports findings. It can also adopt delegated acts specifying criteria and requirements for certification mechanisms and standardized icons, and implementing acts for specifying technical standards for data protection certification and safeguards. It cooperates with supervisory authorities in third countries to develop international cooperation mechanisms regarding personal data protection, specifying formats and procedures for information exchange relating to Binding Corporate Rules and mutual assistance. Member States must notify the Commission of adopted laws and amendments related to data protection provisions, and the Commission receives Supervisory Authority activity reports. The Commission designates gatekeepers regarding Core Platform Services (CPSs) and recognizes adequacy for data transfers. It has legal powers to regulate data sharing under Article 6(11) DMA via an implementing act pursuant to Article 8(2) DMA. It may specify the ineligibility of potential third-party recipients and consult with other bodies to ensure compliance with DMA obligations. The Commission assesses whether a third country provides an adequate level of protection for personal data and sometimes considers the display of advertisements as part of online advertising CPS and other CPS. It receives audited descriptions of profiling techniques from gatekeepers and transmits them to the EDPB. The Commission participates in the Board's activities without voting rights, can designate a representative, and can request matters to be handled within the consistency mechanism, including requesting opinions from the Board. It is informed of Board decisions and receives communications from the Board Chair. [data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

ragPromptContext: [data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.
[organization] Union (European Union) — The Union refers to the European Union, which has an important public interest.

[data] Authorisation Proof — Proof of authorisation is documentation that gatekeepers should keep to demonstrate that third parties have obtained consent from end users, including the duration of such authorisation.

[person] Employee — An Employee is defined as an individual who is employed by an organization or person, belonging to the legal entity of a data controller or processor. These individuals are typically authorized to process personal data, acting under the authority of the controller. Their access to personal data should be restricted based on their specific duties and role within the company. Employees may interact with personal data in various ways, such as manually deleting personal data after its retention period in accordance with internal procedures. They can also be subjects whose personal data, such as their name, is processed by services (e.g., a taxi service in an illustrative example). Employee actions can also lead to incidents, such as when an employee of a controller makes a mistake resulting in a data breach, or when an employee of a service provider has their electronic notebook stolen, as depicted in CASE No. 11. While employees generally operate under established authority, there can be exceptional cases where they unlawfully exceed this authority. Furthermore, employees may face pressure concerning consent for data processing.
Employees are individuals within an organization who may have concerns or complaints.
An employee is a data subject who has a relevant and appropriate relationship with a controller, often forming the basis for legitimate interest in data processing within a group of undertakings.

[method] Administrative Arrangements — Administrative arrangements are provisions that can be inserted between public bodies for data transfers, subject to authorization from the competent SA, including enforceable and effective data subject rights.
A mechanism for personal data transfers between public bodies under Article 46 (3) (b) GDPR, subject to authorization from a competent supervisory authority.
Administrative arrangements are alternative instruments for data transfer, such as Memoranda of Understanding, providing protection through commitments.
Administrative arrangements, such as a memorandum of understanding, provide for enforceable and effective rights for data subjects in the context of data transfers involving public authorities.
Administrative arrangements are provisions inserted between public authorities or bodies, including enforceable data subject rights, used as safeguards.
Administrative Arrangements are agreements related to data protection, which a Supervisory Authority can authorize.
[concept] Article 21(1) — Article 21(1) refers to the right of the data subject to object to processing.

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

A business user is a commercial entity or individual that utilizes gatekeeper products or services and may request access to end-user data.

A Business User is a party that requests access to data, including historic and real-time data, and is subject to monitoring by data protection supervisory authorities.

These considerations apply equally to the interfaces on which the end user initially makes a data portability request, authorises third parties to port data, as well as subsequent reminders and authorisation renewals presented by the gatekeeper to the end user. 127. Similarly, documentation and data portability interfaces made accessible by gatekeepers to third parties should not undermine the effectiveness of Article 6(9) DMA, including by the use of incomplete or misleading information about the rights of authorised third parties under Article 6(9) DMA. 4.6 Authorised third parties 128. The role of authorised third parties under Article 6(9) DMA is a key factor in enabling effective data portability and innovation in the digital sector. Gatekeepers can therefore not restrict, in any way, the data portability use cases and business purposes that authorised third parties can pursue with the data they receive under Article 6(9) DMA. 129. Article 8(1) DMA provides that DMA compliance is without prejudice to compliance with other legal obligations, including the GDPR, which provides for the principle of integrity and confidentiality under Article 5(1), point (f) GDPR and the requirement to ensure security of processing in Article 32 GDPR. In particular, gatekeepers are required to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to prevent unauthorised or unlawful disclosure of personal data to unauthorised third parties. 130. As far as organisational measures are concerned, the gatekeeper, within the framework of its onboarding processes,113 can request third parties’ identity details and information on whether, and to what extent, the data to be ported will involve the transfer of personal data outside the EEA to a third country that has not been recognised as providing an adequate level of protection by the Commission (see paragraphs 136 to 138). 131. However, gatekeepers should not make data portability conditional upon the business use case or purpose for which the ported data will be used by the authorised third party. Gatekeepers should also not gather information pertaining to the authorised third party’s compliance measures under the GDPR, including potential administrative or judicial proceedings the third party has undergone in relation to compliance with the GDPR, or whether the third party has suffered breaches of data security in the past. Such information would not necessarily be an indicator of future compliance or the security of an application or related processing, and as such is not strictly necessary to comply with the gatekeeper’s own responsibility under the GDPR. 132. As far as technical measures are concerned, the gatekeeper should establish authentication procedures to ensure that the gatekeeper only processes data portability requests where the end user or a third party duly authorised by the end user are the ones making such requests. Without proper authentication procedures (including to verify the authorisation granted by end users to a requesting third party), there is a risk of disclosure of personal data to unauthorised third persons and thus of processing that breaches Articles 5(1), point (a) GDPR and other provisions of the GDPR, including Article 5(1), point (f), Article 24(1) and Article 32(1) GDPR. 113 Gatekeepers have implemented different processes and systems that enable authorised third parties to receive data under Article 6(9) DMA. Depending on the specific processes or systems implemented by a gatekeeper, third parties may either be onboarded onto these systems prior to receiving end user authorisation, or after authorisation by end users. 133. The GDPR does not specify exact methods for authenticating data subjects. Authentication of the requesting end user will be presumed to have occurred in instances where the end user is already signed in to a user account associated with the relevant CPS or where the end user signs into the CPS as part of an authorisation procedure prompted by the authorised third party. [data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

Processing can be brought within the second part of the definition if there is the likelihood of a substantial effect, not just an actual substantial effect. [concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them.
